text:
B: Hiya, can you hear me alright?
A: Yeah. Yeah, I can hear you.
B: Brilliant. I'm Craig, I'm up in Lancaster. Where are you, mate? Sorry, not mate, er, force of habit.
A: It's alright. Lorraine. Wednesbury, near Walsall.
B: Oh right, Black Country. I've been through on the M6 loads, never actually stopped, which is probably an insult, sorry.
A: Nobody stops. Don't worry about it.
B: Fair enough. Did you do that puzzle at the start? I was rubbish. I kept going back and changing them.
A: Erm, I did it. I don't know if I did it right. I don't see what it's got to do with anything, to be honest.
B: No, me neither. I think they just want to see if you panic.
A: Well I did. So.
B: Join the club. So are you working at the minute?
A: Not at the minute, no. I was a machinist. Upholstery, cushion covers, curtains, that sort of thing, at a place in Darlaston. It shut about eighteen months ago. So I've been sort of... doing these, and walking the dog, you know.
B: Ah, that's rough. Were you there long?
A: Long enough. I liked it. You just got on with it, nobody bothered you as long as your seams were straight. ...Anyway.
B: That sounds like the dream, honestly. I manage a bike shop, so I've got four staff and they're bothering me all day. Well, not bothering. Asking stuff. I'd rather be in the workshop building a wheel, you know, than doing rotas.
A: I saw the bike. In your picture. In the house.
B: Yeah, that's Nadia's favourite thing, the bike in the front room. My partner. She's given up. There's another one in the hall, to be fair.
A: I'd go mad. Our Kieran leaves his football boots on the stairs and I'm at him every day about it.
B: How old's Kieran?
A: Fifteen. Year ten. So he doesn't listen to anything.
B: I was exactly the same at fifteen, my mum'll tell you. Is that your dog in the photo as well? I could see a bit of a head.
A: Bella. Staffie cross. She's on the settee now, she's... oh, hang on, she's looking at the door. She'll want letting out. Sorry.
B: No, go for it, honestly.
A: No, she can wait. She does this.
B: So do you still sew, like at home?
A: Erm, yeah. I've got me old Singer. I do bits for people. Taking trousers up, me mum's curtains. People keep saying I should charge, but you'd have to set it all up, wouldn't you, and I'm no good with all that. Forms and that.
B: I'm the same with the shop's books, I leave it till the last day. But alterations, people round us can't find anyone. There's a woman two streets over and she's booked up for weeks. If you're fast, you'd be fine.
A: I am fast. I'll give you that.
B: There you go then.
A: Mm. It's all very well, though, isn't it. It's the money for the first bit. With the electric what it is.
B: Yeah, no, fair. It's not nothing.
A: What do you do Sundays then, ride the bike?
B: Yeah, long ride, out to the Trough of Bowland usually, then a bacon barm and a pint after. That's basically my whole personality.
A: A what?
B: A barm. Bread roll. Barm cake.
A: It's a bap.
B: It's a barm, Lorraine.
A: It's a bap. Bacon bap, Saturday morning, every week. Gary does it.
B: Right, I'll give you Saturday, but I'm not budging on the —
